text.p: A leading anti-tobacco lawyer is turning over the claims of 1,000 or more smokers to a class-action suit against cigarette makers being handled by another set of lawyers, a colleague said Thursday.

The consolidation will provide tobacco companies relief from the wave of individual court actions by sick smokers. Further, if the class-action suit filed on behalf of Florida smokers scheduled in September fails, Wilner's clients and any other Florida smokers covered by the suit cannot sue again on their own.

Norwood Wilner, who won a $750,000 verdict against RJ Reynolds Tobacco Co. last year, represents 1,413 sick smokers or their survivors claiming injuries from tobacco companies, according to lawyer Stephanie Hartley.
Hartley said Wilner advised all his smoking-case clients of the Engle suit, a class-action suit being pressed by attorneys Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt on behalf of 400,000-500,000 Florida smokers.

Hundreds of the claims have produced individual lawsuits, with Wilner scheduled to try one in August and another in November. Wilner has received nearly 4,000 inquiries from people claiming illnesses caused by smoking, Hartley said.

He recommended that many of his clients pass up the chance for individual trials and allow their claims to be part of the class action, in which a handful of people sue for themselves and a larger group.

The Engle trial, which will decide whether tobacco companies are liable for lung cancer and other ailments smokers claim have resulted from their addiction to cigarettes, is scheduled for trial on September 8 in Miami's Dade County Court.

Hartley said many Wilner clients are joining the class named after a Miami pediatrician with emphysema, to get a quick trial or to avoid deep probing into family medical histories by tobacco lawyers. Many individual cases will not be tried for four or five years, she said.
Wilner has transferred some 50 lawsuits filed in Duval County Court, his local jurisdiction in Jacksonville, to the class action.

Other cases originally filed with Wilner but transferred to other lawyers in Tampa, Miami and West Palm Beach were also among the 1,000 being placed in the Engle suit, she said. Some of the Wilner claims had not yet produced individual lawsuits, she said.
Hartley said Wilner, and the four other attorneys in his firm dedicated to anti-tobacco lawsuits, were not backing away from pressing cases on behalf of individual smokers or their families.
"All these people still have an action pending," she said. "It's just in a different form."

Wilner, an expert in asbsetos litigation and presenting statistical evidence, won national attention last August, when he won a $750,000 verdict for a life-long smoker, Grady Carter, suffering from lung cancer. That verdict is under appeal.
Wilner lost a second trial last month on behalf of another long-time smoker killed by lung cancer and is scheduled to try a case against Reynolds on August 4.
Another suit against Reynolds, Brown & Williamson , a unit of B.A.T Industries of Britain, and supermarket chain Winn-Dixie Stores Inc was scheduled for November, Hartley said.
